title: Sinusitis
subject: Medicine
summary: Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses, usually infectious. Diagnosis relies on history, exam and simple imaging. Management focuses on treating infection, relieving pressure and preventing complications.

sections.p: Sinusitis is inflammation of the mucosa lining the paranasal sinuses. Acute disease lasts <4 weeks, subacute 4–12 weeks, chronic >12 weeks. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by plain‑film sinus X‑ray or CT if available.

Anterior rhinoscopy: purulent nasal discharge, mucosal edema

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, viral upper respiratory infection is most common. Bacterial superinfection follows, often with Strep pyogenes or Staph aureus.

sections.p: Urgent referral needed for facial swelling, vision changes, severe headache, fever >39 °C, or neurological signs. Complications include orbital cellulitis, meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Treat the underlying cause, relieve pressure, and monitor. First‑line antibiotics cover common bacteria; avoid macrolides if resistance high. Use decongestants and saline irrigation.

t.b: Covers Strep pyogenes, Staph aureus, H. influenzae – first‑line in uncomplicated acute sinusitis
Reserve for patients with penicillin allergy or treatment failure

sections.p: Re‑evaluate in 7–10 days; if symptoms persist, consider imaging. Prevent by treating allergic rhinitis, avoiding smoking, and ensuring good hand hygiene.

faq.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of acute sinusitis?
faq.a: Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus are most common in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: When should I order a CT scan?
faq.a: When symptoms persist >4 weeks, or if there are red flags like facial swelling or visual changes.

faq.q: Can I use a nasal steroid spray for acute sinusitis?
faq.a: No, steroids are reserved for chronic or allergic sinusitis; they do not help acute infection.

exam: What is the first line antibiotic for uncomplicated acute sinusitis? — Amoxicillin‑clavulanate; covers common bacteria, safe in pregnancy, low resistance in many settings.
Which red flag would prompt immediate imaging? — Facial swelling beyond sinus borders; indicates possible orbital cellulitis or abscess.
How would you differentiate sinusitis from a dental abscess on exam? — Dental abscess shows tooth pain and cheek swelling; sinusitis shows facial pain over sinus and purulent nasal discharge.
What is the rationale for using saline irrigation in sinusitis? — It mechanically clears mucus, reduces bacterial load, and improves mucociliary clearance.
When is a fluoroquinolone indicated in sinusitis? — Penicillin allergy or treatment failure after 5 days of first‑line therapy.
How would you manage a patient with chronic sinusitis who is HIV positive? — Treat infection, consider fungal causes, ensure ART adherence, and monitor for opportunistic infections.
What complication is most feared in untreated acute sinusitis? — Orbital cellulitis leading to vision loss.
Why is a CT scan preferred over plain X‑ray in chronic sinusitis? — CT provides detailed mucosal and ostial assessment, guiding surgical planning.
